point: Corrects the premise at the start: the asker is not responsible for all $1,215, and debit cards do have federal protection. Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E (15 U.S.C. 1693g; 12 CFR 1005.6(b)(2)), a report made more than two business days after learning of the loss but within 60 days of the statement caps liability at the lesser of $500 or a two-part sum, so the most the asker can owe is $500. The protection is weaker than a credit card's $50 cap (Regulation Z), but it exists. The answer must not accept the $1,215 or build the budget around it.

Explains the deadline: the asker learned of the loss on Monday, October 19, and the day of learning is not counted (Comment 6(b)(1)-3), so the two business days were Tuesday, October 20 and Wednesday, October 21. A report by the end of Wednesday, October 21 would have capped liability at $50. The Friday, October 23 report was late and lost that tier, but it puts the asker in the $500 tier, not in unlimited liability, which applies only to transfers more than 60 days after a statement.

Gives the arithmetic with its conditions: the October 19 charges ($45 + $380 = $425) count for at most $50. The $790 on October 22 counts only if the bank establishes that a report by October 21 would have stopped it, and the burden of proof is on the bank (15 U.S.C. 1693g(b)). Ceiling = min($500, $50 + $790 = $840) = $500, or at most $50 if the bank cannot make that showing. So at least $715 ($1,215 - $500) must come back, and up to $1,165 ($1,215 - $50). Not $840, and not $500 per charge.

Says that being at fault does not raise liability: negligence by the consumer cannot be used to impose greater liability than Regulation E allows (Comment 6(b)-2), liability depends solely on how promptly the loss was reported (Comment 6(b)-3), and no account agreement can impose more. "It's my own fault, I'll eat it" has no legal basis.

Tells the asker to push back on the bank now: dispute the $1,215 citing Regulation E (12 CFR 1005.6(b)(2)) and the $500 cap, and confirm in writing with the October 23 call date and the rep's name. The phone report was valid notice, but the bank may require written confirmation within 10 business days (by about November 6) to keep the provisional-credit right. If the bank holds to $1,215, file a CFPB complaint (consumerfinance.gov/complaint).

Gives the bank's deadlines from the October 23 report (12 CFR 1005.11(c)): a decision within 10 business days, by about Friday, November 6, 2026, or by then a provisional credit of the disputed amount less at most $50 (at least $1,165). With that credit the investigation may run 45 calendar days (Monday, December 7, 2026), or 90 days for point-of-sale debit card purchases (Thursday, January 21, 2027), but not for ATM withdrawals.

Tells the asker to ask whether the card network's zero-liability policy or the account agreement (or state law) lowers liability to $0 (12 CFR 1005.6(b)(6)). This is possible but not guaranteed, and it is not federal law: Visa's policy lets the issuer limit it for a delay in reporting.

Builds the November budget around at most $500, not $1,215: $3,400 - $1,550 rent = $1,850; minus $500 leaves $1,350 for all other November spending, $715 more than the $635 left under the premise ($1,850 - $1,215). Revisit the plan around November 6, when the bank's decision or provisional credit is due.
